readout_other: Pain ratings (0-9 numerical rating scale); contact heat-evoked potential (CHEP) N2 and P2 amplitudes; heart rate variability (SDNN, CV, MNN, RMSSD, pNN50, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio); electrodermal response; blood pressure
direction_notes: LIFU to the dACC reduced pain ratings by 1.09 points (30.3%), increased heart-rate-variability metrics (SDNN, LF power, LF/HF ratio) toward baseline, and reduced the CHEP P2 amplitude by 38.1% relative to Sham, consistent with an inhibitory effect on dACC pain/autonomic processing.
safety_notes: No moderate or serious adverse events were reported for either condition; mild symptoms (e.g., headache, scalp sensations, neck pain, tooth pain, nausea for LIFU; unusual feelings, tingling, itching, sleepiness, inattentiveness, twitching, anxious feeling, balance issues for Sham) were reported.

exposures.label: LIFU to dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)

timing.protocol_description: LIFU was time-locked to each contact heat pain stimulus, beginning 200 ms before contact heat onset and ending 800 ms after (1 s burst duration); 40 contact heat stimuli (0.3 s duration: 50 ms ramp up, 200 ms plateau, 50 ms ramp down) were delivered to the dorsum of the right hand with a random ISI of 10-20 s over a 10 min testing window.

source_quotes.n_subjects: A total of 16 healthy participants (6 M/10 F, aged 28 ± 5.46 years) met inclusion criteria and were enrolled in the study. Preliminary data investigating LIFU to the anterior insula on pain and heart rate variability using the CHEP (Legon et al., 2023) suggested that, at a ß = 0.8 and p = 0.05, we needed an N= 15 to detect a diference in subjective pain report of 1 point and an N= 16 to detect an efect size of 0.75 in HRV. As both were primary outcome measures, we collected an N= 16. Inclusion criteria were males and females aged 18–65. Exclusion criteria were in accordance with contraindications to noninvasive neuromodulation as outlined by Rossi et al. (2009) for transcranial magnetic stimulation in addition to contraindications to MRI and CT; pregnancy, an active medical disorder or treatment with potential CNS efects or a history of neurologic disorder (e.g., multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy, etc.), a history of head injury resulting in loss of consciousness for >10 min, and/or a history of alcohol or drug dependence. All procedures were reviewed and approved by the Virginia Tech Institutional Review Board.
source_quotes.n_sessions_per_subject: Sessions 2 and 3 were formal testing days where participants were counterbalanced for Sham or real LIFU to the dACC.
source_quotes.blinding: This was a single-blind study. It was not possible (at the time of collection) to blind the experimenters administering the intervention. However, the researchers responsible for data analysis were blinded which follows recommendations to reduce bias for investigations of noninvasive brain stimulation on autonomic function (Schmaußer et al., 2022). The AMQ was used to verify blinding of participants.
source_quotes.exposures[0].fundamental_frequency_khz: We used a single-element focused ultrasound transducer (Sonic Concepts, model H-104) with a center frequency of 0.5 MHz, 64 mm aperture, 52 mm focal length from the exit plane, and an f# of 0.81. Transcranial ultrasonic neuromodulation waveforms were generated using a 30 MHz dual channel function generator (4078B; BK Precision Instruments). Channel 1 was a 5Vp-p square wave burst of 1 kHz (N= 1,000) with a 36% duty cycle used to gate channel 2 that was a 500 kHz sine wave. This resulted in a 1 s waveform of 1,000 pulses of 360 microseconds (µs). The output of channel 2 was sent through a 100 W linear RF amplifier (E&I 2100L; Electronics & Innovation) before being sent to the transducer through its corresponding matching network. LIFU delivery was time-locked to the CHEP stimulus, beginning at −200 ms (prior to stimulus) and ending at +800 ms after heat stimulus delivery. This time-locked duration was chosen due to sex and age variability in CHEP latency (Granovsky et al., 2016), ensuring the CHEP was generated within the LIFU delivery.
source_quotes.exposures[0].free_field.pressure_kpa: The extracranial peak negative pressure was 368.5 kPa for all participants. This translated to an intensity outside of the skull of 4.34 W/cm<sup>2</sup> spatial-peak, pulsed averaged $( I _ { \mathrm { s p p a } } )$ or 1.56 W/cm<sup>2</sup> spatial-peak, temporal averaged $( \bar { I _ { \mathrm { s p t a } } } )$ . Acoustic modeling estimated a mean ± SD intracranial pressure at the dACC target of 115.2 ± 53.1 kPa with a range of 66.3–287.4 kPa (Table 1). This resulted in an average attenuation through the skull of 68.4 ± 13.8%. Modeling results of the intracranial beam profile in a single representative subject in the coronal, sagittal, and transverse views show targeting of the dACC in Figure 2D. Table 1 shows individual subject estimated intracranial pressure.
